utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. This is case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everybody, the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and also the witness. I'm now going to give the floor to the registrar for three IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Several parties have submitted documents to be tendered through witness Miro Salcin. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 430. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 341, and the list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 342. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very well. The Defence has thus one hour in total, and I'm giving the floor to the first Defence team who will have 10 minutes unless they ceded their time to another team. Who is going to start? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions for this witness. We have given our time to the Stojic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have given our time to Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President -- or good afternoon, Mr. President; good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Let's me begin by asking you, when you were being proofed by Ms. Gillett, did you need the assistance of a language assistant?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I take it that you were speaking English back and forth?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Good. And perhaps you can switch into English and you need not worry about waiting for the translation so we can go much quicker.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interrupt, but this matter was discussed in proofing, and albeit that this witness is comfortable enough in proofing to discuss matters in English, it is critical that when he's under oath in court he understands word or word what is being asked of him and is able to give precise answers in his own language. He has never had any formal training in English. He is self-taught, and it is his right to choose to hear in his native language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I just wanted to recall, Mr. Karnavas, that some of us can follow the English directly. But the translation is nevertheless necessary for B/C/S and French, and if we do it with translation it is the danger of running away, to the detriment of our poor interpreters, increases. So I don't think it would be a great gain in time, but I appreciate your effort to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let -- but let me just stick with that -- that issue. As I understand it, in 1994 you worked as a language assistant for UNPROFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And while you were working for UNPROFOR in 1994 as a language assistant, at the same time you were still attached to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say -- okay. Would it be fair to say that your first and foremost employer at the time or your allegiance to, let me put it that way, would have been the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to perform all my duties honourably, professionally, and as well as I possibly could no matter whom my employer was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But that wasn't -- that wasn't the question I posed, you see. So if we're going to let you listen to the B/C/S translation, and we have some marvelous translators here, they're superb, and they make sure my questions are translated precisely. If I can get a precise answer from that -- let me give you the reasons why I'm asking this question. You're working -- you are attached or you are a member of the army of BiH at the same time you're employed by the United Nations. So the question that's begged is: Are you giving information that you learn from UN meetings to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Now, staying again with the language translation issue, as I understand it, when you volunteered and later was mobilised with the ABiH, at the same time there were times at least when you were also employed by various news organisations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So again the question that's begged to be answered is if you are a soldier, albeit not with a weapon but with a camera, how is it that at the same time you're employed by the news agencies? Because this is a rather delicate and sensitive matter, is it not?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you give me a couple of minutes, I could explain this more precisely. Very well. I was indeed a member of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as I emphasised yesterday, I was not involved directly in war-related activities, in combat activities. I also emphasised yesterday that even as a photographer I was not allowed to follow the combat activities of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That very fact tells you that I had enough spare time that I spent for the most part on the premises of the press service of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the agreement with the competent superiors, they gave me authorisation that whenever foreign reporters come to our municipality I would be allowed to work for them, of course with the go-ahead of my superiors, and that indeed happened that way more than once. I worked once for the BBC team, Roger [as interpreted] Bowen. I worked for Maggie O'Kane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the counsel who is asking you questions is using the word "employee," you were employed, and we here on the Bench are legal experts, lawyers. In our minds "employee" means a person who is being paid. Did you receive money from news agencies and those you worked for, including the United Nations, or did the army ask you to help and assist the foreigners as a language assistant working from B/C/S to English and vice versa, or were you paid by the UNPROFOR and the news agencies? So these are two alternatives. Either the ABH asked you to perform certain services for international organisations and the news agencies, or you were paid by the latter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not paid. I was officially employed, hired by the news agency. There were no vacancies that I could apply for, and there is no paper that confirms my work for them as a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So with those news agencies, it was the ABiH who told you go ahead and work for them, but under oath you also say that you were never paid for that work, not by the media.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Officially, no. There were some perks such as free telephone calls to my family abroad, and on one occasion I have to stress that Ms. Maggie O'Kane paid for me, if I remember correctly, 30 German marks for three days of work, and that's only because she insisted. I worked for several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about Jeremy Bowen? Because I believe you said earlier you said a Roger Bowen but we're talking about Jeremy Bowen?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did he pay you?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about for the photographers that you took? Because as a freelancer -- obviously one of the things freelancers do is they try to sell their work to various newspapers. Did you try to sell your photographs?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I tried to sell them but without success.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was because by the time they -- you were able to get them out of the country the material was, for lack of a better word, dated, old?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not get that material out of the country ever. If you remember, I spoke yesterday about my work with Mrs. Maggie O'Kane. I tried to forward that material to Sarajevo on her behalf, but there was a blackout in Sarajevo and it couldn't be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one last question on this matter. What about when you were working for UNPROFOR? Were you getting a salary there?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation with them was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's a -- it calls for a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an official test.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Super. All right. Now, let me move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Apparently the transcript doesn't reflect that the gentleman indicated yes, that he was getting paid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. Witness, our transcript does not reflect what you said. Did UNPROFOR pay you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will repeat. I was paid by the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how much per day did you receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't recall. I think at that time it was a monthly salary, not a per diem, and I think that in that period we were paid around 400 to 500 German marks per month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me move on to something else now. While you were working with these -- these foreign journalists, were you able to take them anywhere they wanted to go or did you have to get pre-clearance from your superiors at the ABiH as to what you could actually show them?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked sometimes as a link, as liaison between foreign reporters and representatives of the army. If foreign reporters expressed the wish to visit some area, I could not give them that approval. I had to convey their wishes to superior officers and tell them what the reporters were seeking. Depending on the situation, the qualified people decided whether and to which demarcation lines the foreign reporters could go, and I never went alone with them. We always had escorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So in other words, aside from assisting these reporters, you are also informing the authorities of ABiH where -- where these -- these reporters, these journalists wanted to go and what they wanted to see, and of course the ABiH through you was able to also, to some extent, curtail or decide what, if anything, these reporters would actually see versus what was actually out there for them to see and to report.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, from reading your statement it indicates - I'm going to skip ahead a little bit - that -- at one point you talk about the Jablanica Museum and that there were Muslim refugees there and that there were Croat refugees as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, with the proviso that that paragraph - I believe it's 17 - does not relate to the same period as the previous paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It relates to a period of several months after August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you for pointing that out, and that clarifies that point, but I notice in your statement, I notice that the Prosecution conveniently omitted to bring this out on direct examination, that at least in your statement you indicate that the Muslim refugees were placed in the cinema hall where they had comfortable chairs and the floor was carpeted versus the Croat refugees where they were placed in the exhibition hall where it was empty and the floor was covered with granite tiles; is that correct? That's in paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But if you give me a minute, I can clarify that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not interested in clarification. I just want to point out that this is what you indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You know, if Mr. Scott wishes to object, he can go ahead and object. He doesn't need to assist his colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in -- on paragraph 17 you also mention about --

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt but there was no such interchange between Mr. Scott and myself, but you should be allowing the witness to answer the question if you've put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You can do that on redirect, madam. You had a responsibility to bring this out on direct examination, and you chose not to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You didn't have such requirement or duty at all. Your Honour, this is absurd. It's a waste of time. If this is the best cross-examine use -- use of cross-examination time that counsel has, we're wasting time. It is -- it is not a Defence to any charge in this case. Is it a defence to any charge in this case how -- where the Croat refugees were kept in Jablanica? The answer is no, and we're wasting time and that is an unfair attack on my colleague, and I for one am not going to sit here and allow it to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, sir, you talk about -- in the same paragraph, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas. I think that you did not have the intention to attack whoever, but you are asking the witness whether it's correct that the Muslim refugees were in a more comfortable area that was carpeted, whereas the Croat refugees were sitting on granite tiles, and the witness answered, "yes, but I can explain." So if you're asking that question, that means you have some sort of idea. He wants to shed some light on it. Why not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to shed that much light on it. I think what is clear is that one set of refugees are given the carpet and comfortable treatment versus the other refugees of another ethnicity or national are given a different treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the relevance of that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You will see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, there is both granite and carpet in this Tribunal, and I don't think that either area in itself constitutes discrimination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was that -- Mr. President. Mr. President, why didn't they put them together in the same place? Why didn't they mix them? Why did they separate them? Why give one preferential treatment over the others? And in the statement, we also note -- notice that the Croats were guarded -- were guarded. The Muslims were not guarded, the Croats were guarded. That's my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please explain, Witness, why was this difference made between Croats and Muslims? You were there. Could you indicate the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried 10 minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I thought. Please give us the reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Muslim refugees who were placed in the movie theatre had arrived to the municipality of Jablanica in the summer of 1993. At that time, the most appropriate way, in the eyes of the authorities - whether civilian or military, I don't know - of accommodating those refugees was to provide them with the most comfortable area, if you can call gyms and movie theatres comfortable. So all the refugees that were flowing in from various areas of Herzegovina were placed in the movie theatre of the Museum Jablanica, in the gym of the primary school, and similar premises on the territory of Jablanica municipality. The Croat refugees that I mentioned in my statement were refugees who had arrived in Jablanica or had been brought to Jablanica several months after the Muslim refugees. As a result, the places of accommodation available were getting more and more crowded, and the new refugees had to be placed somewhere else. Why the separation? There was a war going on, gentlemen, and you could not expect the refugees that had been expelled by HVO soldiers from their homes and the refugees, on the other hand, who had come from their villages on the ABH territory who were deprived of all their possessions, you could not expect these two groups to be placed together. I suppose that it was the most appropriate thing to place those refugees in the museum, and I believe the only available place at that time was the one that they were put in, and the guards at the entrance, as I was informed at the time, were there to protect those Croat refugees from possible reactions by civilians or anyone else. The purpose was to place them in a safe place and to protect them as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a good example why we don't give witnesses time to explain because when I have limited time for cross-examination - and I can't do a proper cross-examination because of time limitations which are unrealistic - we cannot have these sorts of explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But getting to this explanation, I noticed that when it comes to Muslim refugees --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, counsel. There is no need to exaggerate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not exaggerating, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You attacked -- you are referring to problems of discrimination. The witness answers you giving an explanation. It was you who raised the problem. Let the witness answer. And as the witness does not support your theory, you launch yourself into another argument saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the contrary. Mr. President, with all due respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- here is the best example that we wasted time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With all due respect, if you want to ask the explanation you can ask it on your own time. That's the whole point. That's why I'm trying to limit myself. If the Prosecution asked it, it's their time. We're here dividing each other's time. My time is not taken off of your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, the questions of the Judges go on the Judges' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But it is like you -- you don't have to complain. This is our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's why I say, if you want the explanation, that's right. I don't want to -- I don't want it, not because it goes contrary to my theory; I don't have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I noticed that when you talk about Muslim witnesses, Muslim refugees, they get expelled. But Croat refugees, they're the ones that just leave. Now, is that -- did I hear you correctly? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were they expelled?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I can explain that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, no. Were the Croat refugees expelled? Yes or no. To your theory, because I saw your answer. It's on the transcript. We have the transcript. When you talked about Muslim refugees, they were expelled. When you talked about the Croat refugees, they left their places. I didn't hear anything about being expelled, being driven out. Are you making a distinction? Yes, no, I don't know?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to tell you the way I see it and according to the information I got. Muslim refugees told me that they had been expelled, and I know that Croat refugees had arrived in Jablanica as a result of combat activities in the territory of Jablanica municipality or more precisely Doljani village. Those civilians simply stayed behind after the HVO soldiers ran into the mountains. The army took responsibility for those civilians, brought them to Jablanica, and placed them on the premises of the Museum, and you can interpret that anyway you see fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure we have your explanation here. Now, I just want to touch on two other areas very quickly. Was -- are you familiar with a decree that was passed regarding the control of information?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean during the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. If you can look at -- if we can pull up 1D 01215 you can look at it. It should be on the screen. This was a decree regarding carrying out control of information during a state of war. Were you familiar with this at all, sir?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Anyway, we'll leave it at that. Now, one other matter. Were -- when Muslim refugees were arriving in Jablanica, were they put into Croat homes to share the homes with the Croats? Yes, no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You didn't -- you didn't see any of that. All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could pull up 1D 01216. Without mentioning the name of the individual who provided this document which we received from the Prosecution, if we turn over to page 5. And you can read the English, so you're not handicapped at all. According to this individual who is from Jablanica, he indicates that apparently the president service of the 44th Brigade was quite active in -- in sort of dispensing information which might be called propaganda. Not in the sense of propaganda as advertising but sort of in a negative sense. Would you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so -- and now you worked for the press services of the 44th Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a photographer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you were -- you also worked accompanying journalists, and as you've indicated, you were the go-between and in a sense the journalists were able -- the ABiH were able to censor what the journalists were able to see and do as a result of you shadowing them as their interpreter; correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you yourself said that I was there as an interpreter, and I behaved like an interpreter. I didn't make any decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you made any decisions at an all. Somebody else made the decisions. But what I'm trying to point out to the honourable members of our Tribunal is that these foreign journalists are seeing what the ABiH wants to see at the exclusion of all the information that's out there, that some of it might portray the ABiH in a negative point or it might be more favourable to the Croats. That's what I'm trying to suggest. And you acted as a go-between, albeit you had nothing to do with that. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part. I know the situation, and I know a situation in which the foreign journalist mentioned yesterday, Eileen, asked my superiors to visit the separation lines, and she wasn't given permission to do so for three days because it was too dangerous. It was only on the third day that she was granted permission and then I accompanied her and I think there were two others, too, two other BiH army members. We accompanied her up to a part of the front line where at that point in time there were no combat activities going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me be concrete here, or somewhat concrete. When you get to paragraph 17 in your statement you talk about -- that there was a gaol in the basement of the -- of the museum that you had no access to; correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You did not -- you did not have access.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I seem to remember, I said that I think there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You say here and I quote: "There was a gaol in the basement but I was never allowed in there."

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know who was in that gaol?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know because I was never in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you say, "I was never allowed." There's a difference. One is never taking the opportunity to go visit. Another one is not being permitted to visit. Now, did any of the foreign journalists, for instance, ask to see where Croat prisoners of war were being held?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, because at least the people I worked with did not have any requests of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, how much time has been used up? You have already overstepped your time by two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You had 10 minutes, plus the 10 minutes given to you, so you have exceeded by two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would nevertheless ask a question to you. Would you -- would you kindly indicate the source of this document? It's a statement by Mr. Zelenika. It is not signed, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. As you can see, Your Honour -- Your Honour, there is a number at the very top, L010 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that would denote, as far as I understand, a document that we received from -- from the OTP. And I'm told that I have five minutes from the Praljak Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sure the OTP will give -- will answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But, yeah. But anyway, this is a document that they have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just very briefly because I've just about finished with what I need to accomplish. In this document it talks about the -- the press service of the 44th Brigade characterising the HVO as pro-Ustasha, pro-fascist; is that correct? Did you hear that or witness it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember just now, but quite possibly there were such comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or that the -- the Croat forces' intent was to erase traces of the Muslims and that the Croats were generally characterised as Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that any attempt was being made of characterising the Croats in general terms as Ustashas, only their extremist parts or the extremist members of the Croatian Defence Council who worked and did the kinds of things that we were all witnesses of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just to -- just to -- to -- staying with this document, it says here the CTV, okay, and earlier it says CTV Jablanica, that was the television station that was over there - correct? - operating at the time.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cable television, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Cable television. It says here on page 5 the CTV programme, or the information provided by the press service of the 44th Brigade of the Muslim army in Jablanica was conceived in such a way to provoke hatred against the Croats among even the most well-meaning Muslims. "Since Muslims were already in Croat apartments it was impossible to sit together in the evening and watch the local news, the local television news programmes." Now, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is how this man sees it. It's his perception of the overall situation, and I really can't remember all the reports that came out by cable television, and I couldn't follow that because I had other obligations to attend to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But let's take it step-by-step. In this little part that I read, it shows that -- that at least Muslims, and I would suspect that they were refugees, were sharing apartments with Croats. In other words, families would move in with families. Now you were in Jablanica. Are you going to tell me -- are you going to sit here and tell me that you were totally unaware of that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly didn't know about that, because you must realise, sir, that -- let me remind you of my statement, that in 1992 I returned to Jablanica, so I couldn't know who was living where, who was -- belonged to what ethnic group and facts of that nature. I just didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You could glean that information, sir, especially someone who is in the press, albeit it with a camera, but nonetheless you're hanging around journalists, and I have some experience in that, but, you know, you're going to get information. So you mean to tell me, from even being in Jablanica, you didn't hear any rumours of refugees being moved into apartments with Croats, especially since the space, the living space, was very limited and people had to make do?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that things like that went on, too, but quite simply I'm saying that I didn't know about individual cases whereby Muslim refugees were brought or, as you say, placed in Croat-owned flats and that they lived together with Croatian families. At that time I wasn't interested in things like that. And the journalists who came didn't ask questions like that. So quite simply you're asking me about something that I wasn't focusing on at the time. It was not of interest to me at that time. So I must say that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. One final question. CTV or Cable TV, was that controlled by or was it -- did it work or associate itself with the 44th Brigade, or was that totally independent? In other words, you know, did the 44th Brigade control or be associated with CTV to get its messages, its propaganda, its spin out?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cable television was staffed by people who had worked in that television station before the conflict, and I know that the press service of the BH army at that time, my colleagues, prepared reports which were broadcast every evening over cable television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So in other words, material that was prepared by the press service of the 44th Brigade would be broadcasted over CTV Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. And finally, I guess CTV, cable TV Jablanica, didn't have the right, the authority or the capability to select what material from ABiH would be put on the air and what would be excluded?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they had that capability or not, I'm not quite sure. I think that there was an agreement between the representatives of the capable television network and members of the press service of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But CTV did not censor the material. I guess that's my -- that's what I'm trying to drive at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's -- and hence the reason, Your Honours, why I introduced the previous document, the decree which unfortunately the gentleman was not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I tried to explain. The members of the press service did prepare video material which physically then they would take, they would take the video cassette to the offices of CTV and that's where this was broadcast from. Now, whether there was any censorship or not I really don't know. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And again, Your Honours, just for your own -- for later on, own purposes, at 1D 01215, I believe Article 4 speaks to that so just make a reference to it for future purposes and I'm sure it will come up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I appreciate you coming here to give your testimony. Thank you, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to ask the usher's assistance in handing this binder to the witness to facilitate our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Nozica, tell me how much time you need.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have my 10 minutes, and I have been given 10 minutes from the Coric Defence, and I think that will be sufficient for me to conclude my cross-examination within the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. You don't have to look at the documents. You can close the folder for the time being. I'd like to follow on from what my colleague was asking you and ask you first of all whether you prepared the photographs and whether your photographs were published with the reports that came out from your unit on local television. Were they broadcast on local television? Did you provide them with your photographs and were they published, broadcast?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that there were such situations because whenever we went out together on an assignment given to us by our superiors I went and my -- and the cameraman went to make video footage, and the journalist went doing his part of the job. So there was no need for the photographs to be incorporated into the reports that were broadcast over cable television at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So what you want to say is that what appeared on that local television station were video -- was video material that was filmed simultaneously with you photographing certain events, because you say, "We usually went together."

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was frequently the case but not always.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, on that critical day, and I'm talking about the 28th of August, because you referred to that during the examination-in-chief mostly, you said in the morning you heard that something had happened in Grabovica, and on your own initiative it you took your camera and went to photograph what was going on; is that right? Together with the journalist Eileen.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What was your motive for going? Did you in fact want to take photographs together with her which you might be able to sell on to other news agencies for money later?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, at that point in time, as somebody whose work was photography, I wanted to go and document, take photographs of what was happening, to photograph people who had been released from prison in this specific case. And of course I seized the opportunity and asked my colleague, the lady, to go with me because I knew that she as a foreign national and as a journalist had the possibility of taking all that material from Jablanica to Sarajevo and to enable the world to see what was happening. And one of the results of this activity was the videotape that we were shown yesterday. As a member of the BH army, I was not in a position to leave Jablanica that quickly and to leave it without being granted permission, which meant that the news agencies wouldn't be interested in any material that was 10 or 15 days old.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can I ask you something? When the Prosecution asked you questions then your explanations at length were very welcome, but when I'm asking you questions, without meaning to be rude and interrupting you, may I ask you to give me brief answers. So I don't want to hamper Their Honours from asking questions or anything like that, but if I need explanations, I'll ask them -- I'll ask for them. So please try and adhere to that. Now, you say that you would -- if you wanted to be granted permission from your command you would have to go there and ask for permission. That would take a lot of time. Whereas in the morning you didn't report to anybody in the command and it was your command and headquarters that would be most interested to have the photographs that you were going to take. You were given this assignment only in the afternoon, and then you went again. So in the morning you went on your own initiative. You say you wanted to document. To document for whom? For the BH army, for the authorities in Jablanica, or for your own personal database and documentation? Who did you want to document this for?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: At that time I behaved like a photographer and as somebody who wanted to document what was going on, what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Bravo. Thank you. That's fine. Now, am I right in saying that when photographs appear like this, photographs that are intended to be sold on the foreign market, I was frequently the object of this kind of work, but anyway, when you want to show photographs like this to the world, do you as a rule choose, if I can say, the worst photographs, because only that kind of photograph can be sold very well to other countries? Is that the general principle when we're talking about war photographs and the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a general principle that newspaper photographs depict action, particularly when there's a war and conflict, and, among others, the worst photographs you can take. That too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On that day did you talk to the people you photographed?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you ask them for their names? For instance, the person that you asked to strip, to take his clothes offer, did you talk to him? Did you ask him where he had been, how long he had spent there, how much weight he had lost? Did you ask him for that them or were you just interested in taking the photograph of a very thin, emaciated man?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the man you saw -- we saw in the photograph yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm talking about the two or three that we saw yesterday when you said that you asked them to strip to the waist.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't ask -- give you the same answer in all three cases. I talked to some of the people that I photographed; others I did not. Others I just photographed and some I talked to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you learn their names? Did you take down their names?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me why not? Because I'm rather surprised by your answer. You're sending out photographs to the world of people whom you say were in concentration camps, and I apologise that I have to say this, I'm not questioning that people did leave these centres or camps highly emaciated; however, you and I both know that through -- in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina there were a lot of people who were thin and emaciated because there was just not enough food in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were a lot of thin people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would that not have been a profession and moral obligation to ask who the person was? And now it would help had us to establish what you have improvised to a great extent when you say that some came a little earlier when explaining why some people were thinner and some people were not so thin. You said that some people were there for a longer or shorter period of time, but if we had the names of these people then that would have been a nice gesture towards these people. They would have felt more dignified, and anybody checking out those photographs could establish who the people were. So wouldn't it have been a good idea to ask them for their names?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, possibly from your point of view, but it was not my intention to conduct and investigation at all. All I did, and that was just my job, to take photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you took the kind of photographs that you thought you would be able to sell to the world best?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Photographs that would represent the situation that I encountered when I was there to take the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I apologise, sir. Can you tell me when approximately you had learned that Muslim refugees arrived at the museum in Jablanica? You say they had arrived from various areas of Herzegovina and you said it was in the summer of 1993. They came first and they occupied this hall.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe those are the refugees who came that day, that summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to follow your logic. You said it was the 28th of August, 1993. A moment ago you said to my colleague, Mr. Karnavas, Muslim refugees referred to in paragraph 17 were described in retrospect several months later.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And then you say those Muslims had come earlier. And then they occupied this movie theatre, whereas Croats arrived later. So they were placed in the conditions that have been described. Can you tell me whether you had any knowledge that there were prisoners of war and possibly civilians in the prison in Jablanica? Did your work help you to learn that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew there were prisoners there, but I did not inquire who they were. Nor did anyone ask me to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I am going through what you wanted to convince us of, that your curiosity led you to go to Grabovica and see. Didn't your curiosity take you elsewhere in Jablanica to see whether the prisoners in Jablanica were perhaps in the same situation as the one you photographed elsewhere, even if nobody asked you to? Weren't you curious?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to go where I went and make photographs I didn't need any sort of permission. But to go into a prison, you can only imagine the kind of paperwork and authorisations I would have to obtain. So I did not even try to get all the permits that would allow me to go inside. I just didn't do that. I worked as a photographer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Photographer.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I can imagine the procedure, but did you try to ask anyone?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You didn't even try. That's something different. You did not display any professional curiosity. In hindsight does it seem as logical as it seemed then?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, do you think the same way today? You say that you are a freelance photographer, somebody who is supposed to help in establishing the truth. Does it seem logical today that you were trying to establish the truth what was going on with one ethnic group although there were three of them living in your territory? Did you try to learn anything more about the suffering of other people in that same area? You don't have to answer. We can move on to something more specific, but I would like to get something out of you, because you did go into a lot of things that did not make part of your profession and your area of expertise. You talked about how people behaved, how one could see from their appearance that they had gone through a lot of suffering, and it does kind of fit into propaganda. I'm asking you from the 28th of August, 1993, until the end of the war, did you ever photograph any refugees, prisoners, women, children, Croats, or Serbs who were or had been in prisons held by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the museum in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You photographed them? Whom?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croat refugees I mentioned in my statement and let me add that I did not ask for permission. I went there on my own initiative and --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Refugees or expellees?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm talking about prisoners.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us go through this binder to deal with some facts and dates that you mentioned. 2D 00408, please. We have it all, and it will be placed in e-court, but I would like you to have a look first. I marked the whole document for you. It will be easier to review that way. And the first page is -- that I'm interested in have been translated into our language. This is a document of the 44th Mountain Brigade; is that correct? Municipal Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From Jablanica, the 1st of September, 1993. Your copy is not so good, but you have to take my word for it, it is legible. And it says: "Please find attached a list of prisoners of war with all their personal details, and they are in the collection centre at the museum in Jablanica." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we just look at the number of these people? There were 50 prisoners -- 52 prisoners of war. Is this correct? It's confirmed by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was after the events of the 28th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you know that at the time when you were going to photograph people who were coming from Mostar and Herzegovina, did you know that it was an exchange, all for all?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: No. Your army did not inform you? They did not inform you when those HVO members were exchanged later so you could go and photograph them?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at another document. 2D 00410. Please, this is the battalion of the military police of the 3rd Corps. You can see that it's of the military police battalion, Jablanica company, 5th August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My copy is bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will read slowly. If there is anything in dispute, we can go into detail. Please look at the ELMO. It is a bit clearer on the ELMO. It says: "Subject: List of persons currently at the museum of Jablanica and who were not HVO members." These are civilians.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Look, on the 5th of August, 1993, they were already at the museum in Jablanica, and you told us a moment ago that those Bosniaks, Muslims, of the 28th of August, 1993, had come first to the museum. This document tells us otherwise, and it's only logical, I must say, because we saw from the previous list that those people were mainly from Doljani. It's logical that they had arrived first. Can we conclude -- and this is an army document about civilians. Can we conclude that these 87 civilians were in the prison of the Jablanica museum before the photographs you make? Does that follow from these documents?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it follows.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Another thing you said yesterday was that the place where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I do not see the word "prison" here. Maybe I have not looked correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me to proceed, you will see where it is written that there was a prison, but I can clear it up with the witness if you allow me. Do you allow me?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In this acronym SRZ, what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You really don't know. Would it be logical that the last letter, Z, means Zatvor, prison? Tell me, what was the name of that place where the refugees were put up, as you say Croats who had a guard outside the door? What was that place?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an exhibition hall that before the war served to exhibit artefacts from the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you SRZ is not an exhibition hall certainly. Please, can you tell me, what was the name of the area where the prisoners of war were? It's in the centre of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What was the name of that prison where Croat prisoners of war were placed?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't know where the prisoner of war were. When I came to the museum I saw a guard outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Outside of what?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the hall --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And we're talking about two months after the August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's not play with words. Ms. Nozica, your time has expired by one minute and more. He already said at the beginning that there were prisoners in Jablanica who were guarded by the BH army. What is the purpose of spending more time on it? I would allow it, but you are wasting time. It seems completely useless to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it is devoid of purpose, with all due respect. I just want to see if all the rest that this witness told us is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What rest? What -- what rest are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me just one more document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at 2D 00409. It's a list of children who were taken from Doljani on the 28th of July, 1993, by the Muslim army. The children were locked up in the museum in Jablanica-prison. This is a document of the HVO of the 28th of August, 1993. Do we see that there are 59 children on the list?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we look at this list and see that in the left column there are children born in 1990, 1992, and there's even one baby listed in handwriting?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If we compare this to 2D 00410, we see that the largest number of these children were in fact included in that list. That includes all the civilians who were kept in Jablanica. Does SRZ stand for a collection centre for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the name for the places where the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina held either incarcerated prisoners of war or civilians? You were very frequently in the company of journalists. You possibly visited such places. Tell me, what was the name of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina for such places?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was always called the museum. There were no special names, detention centre or prison or whatever you are trying to insinuate.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And the places where, as you say, the Muslims were locked up, you called them concentration camps.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I think that --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I know you want to elaborate, but you don't know what the conditions were like inside the premises of the museum where those people were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't even say that it wasn't a concentration camp, if you insist.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you would allow that this place where Croats were locked up was also a concentration camp?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't want to go into it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My last question. Please, you said a moment ago you allow the possibility that reason those places where Croats were imprisoned, including prisoners of war, was a concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have used seven minutes more than you actually had. Mr. Praljak, as you have given -- registrar, please give us an account. Yes, you can go ahead, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Malovic.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I have just a few brief questions. Could the usher please take these things to the ELMO and a small magnifying glass. It's a very small map. I need you to look at something and mark it. While it's on the way, I want to ask you this: Have you ever heard of Trusina, Trusina village in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard, but I have no idea what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, very briefly. We have no time. Do you have any information that after the activities of -- and actions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina 23 Croats were killed in Trusina village?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you never went to photograph there because you don't know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just said it was Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But you said that --

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally I went.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that a foreign reporter had been to Trusina, filmed something? Do you know whether it was ever published something -- published anywhere?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you hear about the crime in Doljani?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: After the combat activities, when it was no longer dangerous for you, when there was no risk of you losing your equipment and its secrets, did you get permission to go there and film?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did ask for permission, but I didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that a single foreign reporter did get that permission and filmed what happened in Doljani?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in those few days after the return of the HVO to Doljani nobody, no foreign reporter went there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have you ever seen films or photographs from Doljani in your life?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on Croatian television.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We can repeat the same questions about Grabovica. You know about Grabovica, what happened there. Have you been there? Has a foreign reporter been there? Was it ever broadcast?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered all these questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you don't know. Nobody went or --

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. There was a foreign reporter in Grabovica. I took her there. I was in Grabovica. Films were made, photographs were made and sent on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Have you heard about Neretva 93 operation where a large number of the officers of the BH army was in Jablanica or around Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that operation, but I cannot tell you anything more about it. I just know something was going on, because such information didn't go down to lower levels.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know Sefko Hodzic, at least as a name? It was a journalist who was following that operation and then wrote a series of articles for the Oslobodjenje newspaper.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the name. It's possible that I even met with him in Jablanica, but I really can't remember the details. I suppose that we could have met, because as a journalist he could go. He had access to the press service, but there were other people employed in the press service who liaised with journalists who were not foreigners.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, the local television, do you remember -- did you see on that television station anything that happened in Trusina and the surrounding villages, Konjic, Grabovica, Doljani? Anything? Did you see anything broadcast on that local television station?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that they rebroadcast some HTV footage by cable television.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Look at that first photograph. It is one of your own photographs, is it not?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And it was taken where?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The location is Grabovica, more specifically the hydroelectric power -- or, rather, hydro-electric dam at Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And you were told that the smoke we see there, the blaze we see there, was caused by the incendiary bullets?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Anti-aircraft units firing this kind of bullet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you just sign the photograph and I'm ask for an I contribution number. That's customary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour could I just inquire as to relevance of this? If it's only tu quoque that's not a defence. There is absolutely no relevance to any of this information. It's a complete waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not turned on].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Because it's irrelevant, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not turned on].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why was it brought out yesterday by the Prosecution. He should monitor his own lawyers. Today he's saying it's irrelevant. Yesterday it was relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That is the lead of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not turned on].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Testimony was elicited --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, both of you. Stop there. Mr. Praljak, I have the impression -- well, where's the relevance? Ask your question so that we can understand, because for the moment I don't understand where the relevance is and where you're going with your questions. Now, the Defence time has expired already, so finish off with a general question so that he can answer and we can see where you're going, where all this is leading. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: May we have a look at the next document, the map. It's very simple. I want to establish how far this first place is away from the front lines of the HVO. Turn the map round, please, in the proper way. Take up the magnifying glasses, and I -- put Vrde as the first point, Dreznica is number 2. Do you agree with me there or not?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't agree or not because I really don't know where the separation lines were and where HVO trenches were and where the BH army was. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You said they were released at Vrde, where -- that means where the HVO ceased to be, which is the first red line.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you say so then I must take it as being so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And the second point is Dreznica, that's what it says. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And 3 is Grabovica. Do you see that? Is that correct? Use the magnifying glass. Take a closer look.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you marked the area which is called Diva Grabovica which is at a distance 5 kilometres away from the Grabovica hydroelectric power plant, round the mountain bend going west towards mount Cvrsnica, and this is a village. What you've marked is a village.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I know that, sir. But tell me, from Dreznica to Grabovica, how many kilometres is that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's about five kilometres give or take one kilometre, as the crow flies. Perhaps less even. But you can see that and calculate it from the map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, you can use the map, but tell me, is there any visibility in the depression from Grabovica towards the hills? When you were standing there, can you see anything from those hills?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not from the depression but from the place where the flames were then I suppose you can, although I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. We just sign the map, put your name to the map. This can be calculated on the map, the number of kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think we have accepted that witnesses sign documents, maps, pictures on which they have marked something, but here the witness did not mark anything. So it is for you to introduce this as a means of evidence, but I see no reason at all here why the witness should sign something just because he has looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't agree with your observation in full. The IC number is a number given in court with respect to exhibits that were presented and which are not already recorded in collections of exhibits including e-court. That's the only way in which when later on we come to read the transcript we know what the witness looked at. Those of us who are reading or -- the transcript or anybody else. And I think that this document can be given an IC number.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I don't object to the IC number, nor do I take a stand on admission. I only object to the signing, because there I really see no reason whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution entirely agrees with Your Honour's observation, and it's exactly why I was on my feet, although I had some difficulty with the microphone. There is no reason for the witness to sign this. He has identified nothing on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have an IC number for the map without any signature or initials. Mr. Registrar, an IC number for the map, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be given Exhibit number IC 433, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have exceeded your time limit. Your time is up. What is it you would you like to ask? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to mark Grabovica, Dreznica, and Vrde, because he mentioned this. So he can put numbers 1, 2, and 3 on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, would you please mark Grabovica, Vrde, and the third locality on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Gillett, it is I who do the deciding. Sit down, please. Witness, mark on the map Grabovica, where Grabovica is, which Mr. Praljak would like you to do. Put a 1 for Grabovica, Dreznica number 2, and Vrde number 3. So put 1, 2, and 3 on the map, please, by those places.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to place the hydroelectric power plant of Grabovica, the Donja Grabovica village, or Vrde Grabovica, because this is a large area and these are all different things?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, what do you want marked? We're wasting time on a matter that has absolutely no interest to us, but if you want him to mark the localities we're going to waste even more time. So tell him what it is exactly you wish him to mark on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but I'm going to stand and defend my colleague. This is like showing someone a map of Bosnia and said can you mark this -- put a circle around Sarajevo. Of course it's on the map. Everyone can read it. It's on the map. Why does this witness need to mark what's on the map? I'll agree that -- if someone shows me a map, I will agree those -- where the towns are. I'll agree where Sarajevo is. I'll agree where Mostar is. This is a complete waste of time. My goodness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My last question. You said yesterday and I quote: "The situation in Jablanica was changeable. It changed every day depending on the news, depending on radio and television and the rumours spread." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it then true and correct that by selecting the news and information and deciding how much news you're going to put out you could change the structure and method of thinking and therefore fan the flames of war or reduce them?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all televisions do that. HTV, Jablanica television, CTV, and everything else. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any re-examination from the Prosecution? But before that I see the Petkovic Defence on their feet. The Defence time has already expired. It expired five minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that every Defence team has its own time, and the time of the Defence isn't added together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said that you have one hour, that the Defence has one hour, it was up to you to divide that time up amongst yourselves, and since you haven't done that, then I'm going to ask the registrar to do the calculations of the times used. So this is a problem that you have to deal with, and you have to decide. Now, what is it? What relevant question do you wish to ask at this point, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just say that each of my colleagues said quite precisely how much time they have and who allotted what time to somebody else, and nobody said that the Petkovic Defence allotted its time to anybody, and I do have relevant questions so I would like to ask the Court's indulgence for me to be able to ask those questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon. Tell us, please, the press centre you worked in, was it attached to the Municipal Staff of Jablanica or was it attached to the command of the 44th Brigade, or perhaps to something else? Perhaps it was independent, an independent institution.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was attached to the 44th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, about this press centre.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a press service.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This press service, was it a part of a larger organisational unit?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the press service of the 44th Mountain Brigade. That's implied.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What was the title and position of the person who was directly superior to you? Who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was commander or commanding officer of the press service of the 44th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Along the chain of command, who was above him?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think above him was the commander of the 44th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was there a service or a commander or a commanding officer who would be responsible for morale, political issues? Did such a service exist in that brigade?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Within the 44th Mountain Brigade there was such a thing, but it was not possible to appoint a single person to do all of that. I believe this area of work, which we referred to as propaganda, I think was the job of the journalists of the 44th Mountain Brigade. People in the press service had that responsibility. I suppose I did not do that kind of work myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I was interested in, issues of propaganda were the responsibility of the people employed by the press service. Tell me, at one point you said that you were not allowed to go to the front line, and you were not able to film or photograph the combat activities of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was not allowed to take part in combat activities, but I did go to defence lines when there were no such activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me about the other journalists of the press service. Were they able to report on the combat activities of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were able to report based on the information they received.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did they receive such information mainly from the officers of the BH army who directly took part in such activities or coordinated them or were involved in them in any way?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I can't say yes decisively.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The work of journalists and reporters in war conditions is a very large and interesting story, but can we agree that in the conditions of war journalists are not really able to perform their job while meeting all the requirements of their profession? They are not able to check on the story of both sides, and there are, generally speaking, criteria they're not able to meet. There were journalists in the HVO, the BH army, and it goes for journalists working in every army.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the environment in which they work.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The beginning of your answer was "yes," wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The cable television of Jablanica, whose property was it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN MALOVIC [Resumed]
